title: The Slaking Pit
content:
### The Slaking Pit

In Revdanda, the air carries a heavy salt mist that ruins cheap steel screws within months. When I decided to repair the old single-story house I inherited from my maternal uncle, the local contractors suggested stripping the walls down to the brick and coating them with Portland cement and acrylic primer. "Two coats of plastic paint," one of them told me, pointing at a shiny color swatch. "Water won't touch it."

But cement traps water in these coastal villages. The moisture rises from the high water table, gets trapped behind the impervious plastic paint, and eventually pushes the plaster off the brick in bloated, gray blisters.

Instead, I hired Vithal. He is sixty-two, has a cataract beginning to cloud his left eye, and carries an old brass plumb bob in a stained canvas bag. He does not use cement. He uses *chuna*—slaked lime.

### The Chemistry of Slow Curing

For three months, Vithal kept a three-foot-deep pit in the backyard filled with quicklime and water. When quicklime ($CaO$) meets water, it boils violently, releasing heat that can blister skin. This is the slaking process, transforming the volatile stone into a smooth paste of calcium hydroxide ($Ca(OH)_2$).

"If you use it too early," Vithal said, stirring the thick white milk with a bamboo pole, "the unhydrated core will wake up inside your wall when the monsoon hits. It will swell and pop your plaster."

Most modern builders cannot wait three days, let alone three months. But time is the only ingredient that stabilizes the binder. To the slaked lime, Vithal added sharp river sand, crushed brick dust for hydraulic properties, and a fermented decoction of jaggery and *haritaki* fruit. The organic sugars in the jaggery retard the setting time, allowing the plaster to be worked cleanly, while the natural tannins increase its water resistance.

Unlike cement, which sets through a rapid chemical reaction with water, lime plaster cures by absorbing carbon dioxide ($CO_2$) directly from the air. It slowly returns to its original state: calcium carbonate, or limestone. It literally absorbs the air around it to become stone again.

### The Weight of Possessions

While the plaster cured, my belongings sat in twenty-two double-walled cardboard boxes under a tarpaulin sheet in the yard. My books—mostly architectural monographs and historical surveys of Western India—were already beginning to swell at the edges.

I felt the itch of modern haste. I asked Vithal if we could speed up the final coat by adding a small percentage of gypsum or white cement.

Vithal stopped troweling. He wiped his hands on his faded blue shorts and looked at me. He has a habit of clicking his tongue against his teeth when he is annoyed. "If you want a plastic box, buy a plastic box," he said. "The lime needs the air. If you close its nose, it dies."

He was right, of course. My desire to unpack, to surround myself with my library, was an attempt to impose my timeline on a material that operates on its own. The house was teaching me my own hypocrisy. I wrote essays on slow architecture from a laptop while secretly wishing my own walls would dry faster so I could unpack my possessions.

### The Sound of Raw Plaster

By late June, the first monsoon storms hit the Konkan coast. The rain came down in gray sheets, turning the backyard pit into a muddy pool. Inside the house, the walls were still damp to the touch, but they did not smell of chemicals or damp concrete. They smelled of wet earth and sweet jaggery.

I sat on a single wooden packing crate in the middle of the unfinished living room. There were no curtains, no rugs, no bookshelves. The plaster was a pale, uneven cream color, showing the faint marks of Vithal’s wooden float.

When you speak in a room plastered with lime, the sound is different. Cement is dense and hard; it bounces high-frequency sounds back at you, creating a sharp, metallic ring. Lime plaster is porous, filled with microscopic voids that absorb the harshness of your voice. The room felt quiet, not because there was no noise from the storm outside, but because the space itself was soft.

I looked at my boxes under the leaking tarpaulin. A corner of one box had collapsed, exposing the damp spine of a book on Le Corbusier. I left it there. The rain continued to strike the terracotta roof tiles, and the lime walls slowly drew in the damp air, curing in the dark.

---

summary: An exploration of lime plaster, vernacular building traditions, and the psychological cost of modern architectural haste.

title: The Geometry of Two Cups
content:
In Mahanagar, the afternoons do not end; they merely stretch themselves thin like old muslin. My kitchen has two clocks. One is the digital display on the induction cooktop that blinks 16:45 in sharp, sterile red. The other is a round, tin-plated Ajanta wall clock that loses four minutes every week, its ticking a slow, heavy heartbeat against the distempered wall. I keep them both because truth lies somewhere in that four-minute silence—the gap between what is happening and what we are willing to admit.

I am preparing tea for two, though the train from New Delhi is already three hours late according to the National Train Enquiry System. The app tells me the *Shatabdi* is delayed near Kanpur due to track maintenance. I swipe down to refresh the screen, my thumb leaving a faint smudge of ginger-juice on the tempered glass. I hate how instantly we can measure distance now, how we can watch a little blue arrow crawl across a digital map of Uttar Pradesh, stripping the journey of its holy uncertainty.

### I. The Boiling Point

> तुमने कहा था,
> जब पहली बारिश धूल को शांत करेगी,
> मैं लौट आऊँगा।
> अब देखो,
> हवा में सूखी मिट्टी का शोर है,
> और चाय का पानी खौल चुका है।
>
> *(You had said,*
> *when the first rain settles the dust,*
> *I will return.*
> *Look now,*
> *the wind carries the noise of dry earth,*
> *and the water for the tea has already boiled.)*

There is a specific violence in a boiling kettle. The water rises, desperate to escape its own skin. I drop the bruised ginger into the pot. I do not use the steel grater; its clean, sharp teeth slice the root too neatly, letting the juice run wastefully over the counter. Instead, I use the iron *khal-batta*—the mortar and pestle my grandmother brought from Gorakhpur in 1968. It is heavy, dark, and smelling faintly of the dry cumin and coriander it has crushed for half a century. A single, heavy blow. The ginger splits along its fibers, wet and raw.

There is an old promise we made under the shade of the bougainvillea behind the library: that we would never let the tea grow cold while discussing things that cannot be mended. We called it our 'treaty of the third pour.' But promises, I have realized, are like the loose threads of a handloom saree—if you pull them too hard to make them neat, the whole border begins to pucker.

I have kept your cup ready. It is the one with the small chip on the rim, the blue pottery from Khurja we bought because the shopkeeper swore the clay was mixed with the water of the Ganga. It sits next to mine—a modern, double-walled glass cup that keeps the heat inside but feels cold to the touch from the outside. That is my contradiction, I suppose. I want the warmth, but I am too afraid of being burned to hold it directly.

### II. The Evening Tea

> आधा चम्मच चीनी, दो इलायची के दाने,
> और एक पुरानी आदत—
> किवाड़ के पीछे पैर की आहट सुनना।
> गली के बच्चे अब घर लौट चुके हैं,
> पर तुम्हारी परछाईं अभी भी
> सीढ़ियों पर ठहरने का बहाना ढूंढती है।
>
> *(Half a spoon of sugar, two cardamom pods,*
> *and an old habit—*
> *listening for the sound of footsteps behind the door.*
> *The street children have returned home by now,*
> *yet your shadow still*
> *looks for excuses to linger on the stairs.)*

The first drops of rain hit the tin roof of the neighbor’s garage. It is not the grand, dramatic downpour of the movies, but a hesitant, dusty sputter. The leaves of the curry plant on my balcony look tired, coated in a gray layer of summer dust that refuses to wash off easily. I step out to bring in the clothesline. The air is thick, smelling of parched bricks and gasoline from the main road.

I look at my phone again. The blue arrow on the map has stopped near Unnao. A signal failure, perhaps. Or just the world telling us to wait a little longer, to test whether the cardamom in the pot will lose its fragrance if left to simmer on the lowest flame. I turn the knob down. The tea turns a deep, woody amber.

I will not call you. To call is to admit that the distance is real, that the train is not just an extension of my own waiting. Instead, I pour the tea into the chipped Khurja cup, letting the steam rise between us, filling the empty space where your voice should have been.

The steam settles on the windowpane, turning the streetlights into soft, blurry smears of gold.

---

​﻿#writon​
summary: A bilingual reflection on the quiet rituals of waiting, the slow simmer of cardamom tea, and the distance between a delayed train and a promised return.
